Patient-reported symptoms:
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Vignette:
Derek, a 29-year-old Coast Guard officer, still remembers the night that flattened his life into something unrecognizable. It was late autumn, just after a twelve-hour shift patrolling the harbor. He had stopped at a convenience store for coffee and was walking back to his truck through a dimly lit parking lot when two men appeared from behind a dumpster. One pressed a handgun against his ribs while the other rifled through his pockets, taking his wallet, phone, and the department-issued watch his father had given him. They told him not to move for five minutes, then vanished. Derek lay on the asphalt, heart hammering, until the cold seeped through his jacket and he finally scrambled to his feet. He drove home in a daze, said nothing to his girlfriend, and lay awake until morning.

In the weeks that followed, Derek found himself unable to describe what had happened. His girlfriend, worried by his silences, would ask gentle questions. He would open his mouth, but the words felt like they belonged to someone else—flat, hollow, useless. When he tried to force a narrative, his mind went blank, and he would end up shaking his head. The memory refused to be shaped into language; it existed as a jumble of impressions—the cold metal against his ribs, the smell of garbage and wet asphalt, the sound of his own ragged breathing—but never as a story he could tell. Sometimes, when he did let himself replay the scene, he felt nothing at all. He would sit on the edge of the bed, recalling the gun, the threat, the fear that should have been there, and instead feel a strange, dead numbness, as if the whole event had happened to a stranger. That frightened him more than the fear itself—what kind of person could recall being robbed and feel only emptiness?

The memories themselves came in fragments. He would be walking through the Coast Guard station and suddenly see the dumpster, but without context, without the men or the gun. Or he would hear a car door slam and feel the pressure of someone’s hand on his chest, but the rest of the memory would be missing, like a puzzle with most of the pieces lost. These fragments never fit together into a coherent timeline; they arrived uninvited, disconnected, and left him confused and disoriented. He had stopped trying to make sense of them.

His girlfriend, Maria, began to feel the distance. She told him it was like living with a ghost—he was present but unreachable. Their conversations grew stilted because Derek could no longer share what was inside his head. At the station, his colleagues noticed he had become quieter, slower to volunteer for night patrols. He never told them why. He had come to believe that something fundamental in him had broken that night, that his mind had shattered the memory into pieces he would never be able to reassemble.

What finally brought Derek to seek help was a moment during a routine debriefing. A junior officer described a tense encounter with a suspect, and Derek realized he could not recall the sequence of his own mugging in any order that made sense. The panic that rose in his chest—unbidden, wordless—convinced him that he was losing his grip on his own mind. He scheduled an appointment with a psychologist, hoping to find words for what he could not name, and terrified that the fragments he held were all that would ever remain.
